title: Configure AWS CodeDeploy
content:
Step 1: Create an IAM Role for CodeDeploy CodeDeploy needs permission to access EC2 instances and manage deployments.
Sign in to the AWS Management Console.
Open IAM and select Roles.
Choose Create role.
Under Trusted entity type, select AWS service.
Select CodeDeploy as the use case.
Choose the CodeDeploy use case for EC2/on-premises deployments.
Enter the role name:
CodeDeployServiceRole
Create the role.
After creation, open the role and verify that its trusted entity allows the CodeDeploy service to assume the role.
Step 2: Create a CodeDeploy Application Open AWS CodeDeploy in the AWS Console.
Select Applications from the navigation panel.
Choose Create application.
Enter the following configuration:
Application name: cicd-aws-demo-app Compute platform: EC2/On-premises Choose Create application.
The application should now appear in the CodeDeploy application list.
Step 3: Create a Deployment Group Open cicd-aws-demo-app.
Choose Create deployment group.
Enter the following configuration:
Deployment group name: cicd-aws-demo-deployment-group Service role: CodeDeployServiceRole Deployment type: In-place Environment configuration: Amazon EC2 instances Configure the EC2 instance selection criteria using tags.
For example, if the EC2 instance has the tag Name=ci-cd-demo-server, select instances matching that tag. The tag key and value must match the actual EC2 instance.
Choose Create deployment group.
Important: The deployment group will not target an instance unless its selection criteria match that instance. The EC2 instance must also have an appropriate IAM instance profile and the CodeDeploy agent installed and running.
Step 4: Prepare the EC2 Instance Before deploying the application, verify the following:
The EC2 instance is running. The instance has an IAM instance profile that allows it to access the required deployment artifacts and services. The CodeDeploy agent is installed and running. The instance can reach the required AWS endpoints. The application’s security group allows the port used by the web application. On a Linux EC2 instance, check the agent with:
sudo systemctl status codedeploy-agent If the agent is installed but stopped, start it:
sudo systemctl start codedeploy-agent If the command reports that the service does not exist, install the CodeDeploy agent for the instance’s operating system and AWS Region before continuing.
Step 5: Verify the Configuration Before proceeding to deployment, check these items:
The application cicd-aws-demo-app exists. The deployment group cicd-aws-demo-deployment-group exists. The deployment group targets the intended EC2 instance. The service role is selected correctly. The EC2 instance has the required instance profile. The CodeDeploy agent is running. Once these checks are complete, continue to Deploy and Verify the Application.
Result At the end of this section, the CodeDeploy application and deployment group are configured and ready to receive a deployment from AWS CodePipeline or a manually created deployment.

title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpointsContinuous Integration and Continuous Deployment Continuous Integration (CI) is a software development practice in which code changes are frequently integrated into a shared repository and automatically built and tested.
Continuous Deployment (CD) automates the process of releasing application changes to a target environment after the required build and testing steps have succeeded.
AWS CI/CD services help automate the software delivery process, reduce manual operations, and improve deployment consistency.
Workshop overview In this workshop, you will build and deploy a simple web application using Java and Spring Boot. You will use AWS services to automate the build, testing, and deployment process.
“Source Repository” uses GitHub to store the application source code. Changes pushed to the repository trigger the CI/CD workflow.
“Build and Test” uses AWS CodeBuild to compile the application, run unit tests, and generate a deployment artifact. The pipeline stops if the build or tests fail.
“Deployment” uses AWS CodeDeploy to deploy the application to an Amazon EC2 instance. Amazon S3 stores the build artifact used during deployment.
“Monitoring” uses Amazon CloudWatch to collect relevant logs and monitor the deployment process.
The goal is to create a repeatable deployment workflow in which a code change can be built, tested, and deployed automatically.
Expected outcome
At the end of this workshop, you will have a simple web application running on Amazon EC2 and an automated pipeline that builds, tests, and deploys application updates from GitHub.

title: Prepare the Spring Boot Application
content:
1. Check the Development Environment Before building the web application, make sure that Java 17, Git, and Maven are available on your computer.
Open PowerShell or the terminal in VS Code and run the following commands:
java -version git --version To check whether the project includes the Maven Wrapper, navigate to the project directory and run:
.\mvnw.cmd -version If the project does not contain mvnw.cmd, install Maven or configure the project to use an available Maven installation.
2. Open the Project Open the existing cicd-aws-demo project in VS Code.
The project should contain the following main files and directories:
cicd-aws-demo/ ├── src/ │ ├── main/ │ │ └── java/ │ └── test/ │ └── java/ ├── pom.xml ├── buildspec.yml ├── appspec.yml └── scripts/ src/main/java/ contains the application source code. src/test/java/ contains the unit tests. pom.xml defines the Maven project and its dependencies. buildspec.yml contains the build instructions for AWS CodeBuild. appspec.yml defines the deployment instructions for AWS CodeDeploy. scripts/ contains the deployment scripts. 3. Build the Web Application In the VS Code terminal, navigate to the project root directory:
cd "cd D:\cicd-aws-demo" If your project is stored in another location, replace the path with your actual project directory.
Run the following command to build the application and execute the unit tests:
.\mvnw.cmd clean package If the build succeeds, Maven will generate the application package in the target/ directory.
Look for the generated .jar file in that directory.
4. Run the Application Locally Run the Spring Boot application using the generated JAR file:
java -jar target/<application-name>.jar Replace <application-name>.jar with the actual JAR filename generated in the target/ directory.
Open a browser and visit the application’s configured local URL, typically:
http://localhost:8080
If the application starts successfully and the page responds as expected, the local application is ready for the next step.
5. Expected Result After completing this section, you should have:
A working Spring Boot web application. A successful local Maven build. Unit tests executed during the build. A generated JAR package in the target/ directory. Content Push the Source Code to GitHub

title: Proposal
content:
Automated CI/CD Pipeline for Web Application Deployment on AWS 1. Executive Summary This project focuses on designing and implementing an automated Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CI/CD) pipeline for a Spring Boot web application on Amazon Web Services (AWS).
The project uses GitHub to manage source code, AWS CodeBuild to compile the application and execute tests, AWS CodeDeploy to deploy the application to an Amazon EC2 instance, and AWS CodePipeline to coordinate the entire workflow. Amazon CloudWatch can be used to review available logs and monitor relevant resources.
The main objective is to reduce manual deployment steps, improve consistency, and establish a repeatable process for building, testing, and deploying a web application. The project is designed as a practical demonstration suitable for an internship project and can be extended with additional testing, security checks, and monitoring features.
2. Problem Statement What Is the Problem? Manual application deployment requires developers to perform several steps, including retrieving source code, building the application, running tests, preparing deployment files, and transferring the application to a server.
These steps can be time-consuming and may lead to configuration mistakes or inconsistent deployment results. When source code changes frequently, repeating the same process manually also makes it harder to maintain a reliable release workflow.
For a small web application project, a practical automated deployment pipeline can help standardize these tasks and make build and deployment results easier to review.
The Solution The proposed solution is an AWS-based CI/CD pipeline that connects source code management, automated building and testing, and application deployment.
The source code is stored in a GitHub repository. AWS CodePipeline coordinates the workflow, AWS CodeBuild builds and tests the application using Maven, and AWS CodeDeploy deploys the packaged application to an Amazon EC2 instance. The application runs on EC2 and can be accessed through its configured network endpoint.
The proposed workflow is:
GitHub → AWS CodePipeline → AWS CodeBuild → AWS CodeDeploy → Amazon EC2
The build stage uses a buildspec.yml file to define build commands. The deployment package includes an appspec.yml file and the scripts required by CodeDeploy. Amazon CloudWatch can support troubleshooting by providing access to relevant logs and metrics when configured.
Benefits and Expected Value The project provides the following expected benefits:
Reduced manual work: Automates recurring build and deployment steps. Consistency: Uses defined build commands and deployment instructions. Improved traceability: Makes pipeline execution results and logs easier to review. Earlier error detection: Runs configured tests before the deployment stage. Practical AWS experience: Demonstrates the use of AWS developer tools and EC2. Extensibility: Provides a foundation for adding quality gates, security checks, rollback procedures, and more advanced monitoring. The project is intended primarily for educational and demonstration purposes. Actual time savings, reliability improvements, and operating costs should be evaluated after implementation and testing.
3. Solution Architecture The proposed architecture consists of a source code repository, an automated pipeline, a build environment, a deployment service, and an EC2 instance hosting the web application.
Architecture Overview Source Code Management: GitHub stores the Spring Boot source code and configuration files. Pipeline Orchestration: AWS CodePipeline coordinates the source, build, and deployment stages. Build and Testing: AWS CodeBuild uses Maven to compile the application, run configured unit tests, and package the application. Application Deployment: AWS CodeDeploy deploys the application package to the target EC2 instance using the deployment instructions and scripts. Application Hosting: Amazon EC2 runs the deployed Spring Boot application. Monitoring and Troubleshooting: Amazon CloudWatch can be used to review configured logs and monitor relevant AWS resources. AWS Services Used GitHub: Stores source code and tracks changes. AWS CodePipeline: Coordinates the CI/CD workflow. AWS CodeBuild: Compiles the source code, runs tests, and generates the application package. AWS CodeDeploy: Automates application deployment to EC2. Amazon EC2: Hosts the deployed Spring Boot application. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM): Controls permissions for pipeline components and AWS resources. Amazon CloudWatch: Supports monitoring and troubleshooting through available metrics and configured logs. Component Design Source Repository: Contains application source code, pom.xml, buildspec.yml, appspec.yml, and deployment scripts. Source Stage: Retrieves the project source code from GitHub. Build Stage: Runs Maven commands in CodeBuild to compile, test, and package the application. Artifact Flow: Passes the required build output to the deployment stage. Deploy Stage: Uses CodeDeploy to deliver the application package to the target EC2 instance. Application Runtime: Runs the Spring Boot application on EC2. Monitoring: Uses available pipeline results, deployment logs, and CloudWatch data to investigate issues. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases The project is divided into the following phases:
Phase 1 — Requirement Analysis and Architecture Design: Define the project objectives, identify the required AWS services, and design the CI/CD workflow. Phase 2 — Application and Repository Preparation: Review the Spring Boot project, prepare the development environment, and organize the source code in GitHub. Phase 3 — Automated Build and Testing: Prepare unit tests and configure AWS CodeBuild with a buildspec.yml file. Phase 4 — Deployment Environment Preparation: Prepare the EC2 instance, review security groups and IAM permissions, and identify the application runtime requirements. Phase 5 — Automated Deployment: Configure CodeDeploy, prepare the appspec.yml file and deployment scripts, and define the deployment process. Phase 6 — Pipeline Integration and Evaluation: Integrate the source, build, and deployment stages using CodePipeline, review execution results, troubleshoot errors, and document the outcome. Technical Requirements Application and Development Environment
A Spring Boot web application written in Java. A compatible Java Development Kit (JDK) and Maven build environment. Git and a GitHub repository for source code management. Unit tests appropriate to the application’s implemented functions. A pom.xml file defining project dependencies and build configuration. AWS Environment
An AWS account with the permissions required to configure the project resources. AWS CodePipeline for workflow orchestration. AWS CodeBuild for automated builds and tests. AWS CodeDeploy for application deployment. An Amazon EC2 instance configured to run the application. IAM roles and policies with permissions appropriate to each service. Security group rules that permit only the network traffic required by the application and administrative access. Build and Deployment Configuration
buildspec.yml defines the build phases and commands. appspec.yml defines the files and lifecycle hooks used by CodeDeploy. Deployment scripts manage the application lifecycle where required. The build artifact contains the files needed by the deployment process. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline The project is planned around the following milestones:
Week 1 — AWS Fundamentals: Study basic AWS services and identify the services relevant to the project. Week 2 — CI/CD Design: Learn CI/CD concepts and design the proposed pipeline. Week 3 — Application Preparation: Review the Spring Boot project and prepare the development environment. Week 4 — Source Code Management: Organize the project repository and manage source code with Git and GitHub. Week 5 — Unit Testing: Review or write unit tests and prepare the Maven build process. Week 6 — AWS CodeBuild: Prepare the build specification and configure the automated build stage. Week 7 — AWS Environment Preparation: Prepare the EC2 deployment environment and review IAM and network requirements. Week 8 — AWS CodeDeploy: Prepare deployment instructions and scripts. Week 9 — AWS CodePipeline: Integrate the source, build, and deployment stages. Week 10 — Final Review: Review the workflow, examine available logs, document limitations, and complete the internship report. The timeline represents the planned sequence. Actual completion dates and results should be updated to match the work performed.
6. Budget Estimation The project uses AWS managed developer tools and an EC2 instance. The actual cost depends on the selected AWS Region, instance type, resource usage, storage, data transfer, and service pricing.
The AWS Pricing Calculator can be used to estimate costs before deploying the resources:
AWS Pricing Calculator
Infrastructure Costs Potential cost components include:
Amazon EC2: Instance runtime, attached storage, and any applicable public IPv4 or data transfer charges. AWS CodeBuild: Build minutes and selected compute environment. AWS CodePipeline: Pipeline pricing based on the selected pipeline type and applicable usage. AWS CodeDeploy: Deployment service usage; charges may also arise from the underlying EC2 resources. Amazon CloudWatch: Log ingestion, log storage, metrics, and alarms where applicable. Other AWS Resources: Additional storage, networking, or supporting services if required. The final monthly estimate should be calculated using the actual configuration and expected usage. No fixed total is assumed in this proposal because the required resource sizes, usage levels, and pricing details have not yet been confirmed.
To control costs, the project should use appropriately sized resources, monitor usage, and stop or delete resources when they are no longer needed.
7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Build Failures: Medium impact, medium probability. Incorrect dependencies, Java versions, or Maven configuration may cause the build to fail. Deployment Failures: High impact, medium probability. Incorrect deployment instructions, script permissions, or runtime configuration may prevent the application from starting. IAM Permission Errors: Medium to high impact, medium probability. Missing or excessive permissions may interrupt the pipeline or create security risks. Network and Connectivity Issues: Medium impact, medium probability. Security group rules or connectivity problems may prevent access to the application. Unexpected AWS Costs: Medium impact, low to medium probability. Resources left running or usage beyond the estimate may increase costs. These ratings are preliminary and should be reviewed as the implementation progresses.
Mitigation Strategies Build Reliability: Use explicit build commands, run unit tests, and inspect CodeBuild logs. Deployment Reliability: Validate the deployment package, check lifecycle scripts, and review CodeDeploy logs. Access Control: Apply least-privilege IAM permissions and avoid storing credentials directly in source code. Network Security: Restrict inbound access to the ports and source addresses required for the project. Cost Management: Review AWS billing information, estimate costs before deployment, and configure budget alerts where appropriate. Contingency Plans If a build fails, inspect the build logs, correct the configuration, and run the build again. If deployment fails, inspect the CodeDeploy deployment details and application logs, then correct the deployment configuration. If the application becomes unavailable, investigate the EC2 instance and application runtime before attempting another deployment. If resources are no longer required, stop or delete them as appropriate after confirming that doing so will not remove needed data. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements The project is expected to produce a repeatable CI/CD workflow that connects source code management, automated building and testing, and deployment to an EC2-hosted web application.
Expected technical outcomes include:
A GitHub repository containing the application and CI/CD configuration files. An AWS CodeBuild project that builds and tests the application. An AWS CodeDeploy configuration for deploying the application to EC2. An AWS CodePipeline workflow coordinating the source, build, and deployment stages. A documented process for reviewing build and deployment results. A basic approach to monitoring and troubleshooting using available AWS logs and metrics. Long-Term Value The project provides practical experience with CI/CD principles and AWS developer tools. Its architecture can serve as a starting point for future improvements, including additional automated tests, code quality checks, security scanning, approval stages, rollback strategies, and more comprehensive monitoring.

title: Deploy and Verify the Application
content:
Step 1: Prepare the Deployment Files AWS CodeDeploy needs an application revision containing the files to deploy and an appspec.yml file describing the deployment instructions.
In the project directory, verify that the deployment files exist:
cicd-aws-demo/ ├── appspec.yml ├── buildspec.yml ├── pom.xml ├── scripts/ │ ├── install_dependencies.sh │ ├── start_server.sh │ └── stop_server.sh └── src/ The filenames and directory structure in the revision must match the paths specified in appspec.yml.
For an EC2 deployment, the AppSpec file must be named appspec.yml and be located at the root of the deployment revision.
Step 2: Build the Application Build and test the Spring Boot application before deploying it.
From the project directory, run:
.\mvnw.cmd clean test package Check the build output. Maven should finish successfully, and the application JAR should be generated under target/.
For example:
Get-ChildItem .\target\*.jar If the tests fail or the JAR is not generated, resolve the build problem before continuing.
Step 3: Start a Deployment There are two ways to start a deployment.
Option A: Deploy through CodePipeline Use this option when the project is connected to AWS CodePipeline.
Open AWS CodePipeline. Select the pipeline configured for cicd-aws-demo. Choose Release change if the pipeline is not triggered automatically. Wait for the Source, Build, and Deploy stages to run. Open the Deploy stage to inspect its status. The deployment stage should use the CodeDeploy application cicd-aws-demo-app and deployment group cicd-aws-demo-deployment-group.
Option B: Create a Manual Deployment Use this option to test CodeDeploy before connecting it to CodePipeline.
Open AWS CodeDeploy.
Select Applications and open cicd-aws-demo-app.
Select the deployment group cicd-aws-demo-deployment-group.
Choose Create deployment.
Select the appropriate revision source.
For an S3 revision, select the S3 bucket, object key, and version or ETag as required. The uploaded revision must contain appspec.yml at its root.
Choose Create deployment.
Wait for the deployment to finish.
A manual deployment requires a packaged revision uploaded to the selected source. Building a JAR locally alone does not create an S3 deployment revision.
Step 4: Check the Deployment Status In CodeDeploy, open the deployment and inspect its status.
Succeeded: The deployment lifecycle completed successfully. Failed: Open the deployment details and inspect the failed lifecycle event. In Progress: Wait for the deployment to complete before testing the application. Check the lifecycle events to identify whether the failure occurred during DownloadBundle, Install, ApplicationStart, or another deployment hook.
Step 5: Check the Application on EC2 Connect to the EC2 instance and inspect the application process and logs.
For a Linux instance, useful commands include:
ps -ef | grep java sudo journalctl -u codedeploy-agent --no-pager -n 100 If the application writes to a file, inspect the application log at the configured log path.
If the deployment succeeds but the application does not respond, check that:
The Spring Boot process is running. The application listens on the expected port. The EC2 security group permits inbound traffic to that port. The deployment scripts have the correct file paths and executable permissions. Step 6: Test the Web Application If the Spring Boot application is configured to listen on port 8080, open the following address in a browser:
http://<EC2-Public-IP>:8080 Replace <EC2-Public-IP> with the public IPv4 address of the actual EC2 instance.
If the application uses a different port or a specific endpoint, use the configured port and endpoint instead.
If the page does not load, verify the application’s health locally on the EC2 instance and check the EC2 security group and network configuration.
Step 7: Record the Results Record the following information for the project report:
Item Expected result CodeDeploy application cicd-aws-demo-app exists Deployment group cicd-aws-demo-deployment-group exists Deployment status Succeeded Application process Running on EC2 Web access test Application responds at the configured address Capture screenshots of the deployment status, lifecycle events, and successful browser test as evidence for the graduation report.
Troubleshooting Problem What to check Deployment fails before installation Revision source, IAM permissions, and appspec.yml location EC2 instance is not selected Instance tags and deployment group selection criteria CodeDeploy agent is unavailable Agent installation, service status, and network connectivity Application fails to start Script permissions, file paths, Java version, and application logs Browser cannot connect Application port, process status, and EC2 security group Result The application is deployed to EC2 and verified through deployment status, instance checks, and a browser test. Once manual deployment works, the same application and deployment group can be used by AWS CodePipeline for automated deployments.

title: Build with AWS CodeBuild
content:

In this workshop, CodeBuild will retrieve the source code from the GitHub repository, use Maven to build the application, and run the unit tests defined in the project.
Why use AWS CodeBuild? Automated Build: CodeBuild automatically compiles the application without requiring manual commands on your local computer. Automated Testing: Unit tests are executed during the build process to verify the application’s behavior. Build Artifacts: If the build succeeds, CodeBuild generates a deployable application package that can be stored in Amazon S3. CI/CD Integration: CodeBuild integrates with AWS CodePipeline to automate the build stage whenever source code changes are detected. Build Process Overview The build process follows these steps:
Source: Retrieve the application source code from GitHub. Build: Use Maven to compile the Spring Boot application. Test: Execute unit tests to verify the application. Package: Generate the application JAR file. Store Artifacts: Prepare the build output for the deployment stage. Build Configuration The project uses a buildspec.yml file to define the commands executed by CodeBuild.
The configuration specifies the Java runtime environment, the commands to build and test the application, and the location of the generated artifacts.
The build output will be used in the next stage of the CI/CD pipeline.
Expected Result After completing this section, you should have:
An AWS CodeBuild project configured for the application. A build process that uses Maven to compile the source code. Unit tests executed automatically during the build. A packaged application artifact ready for the deployment stage. Content Configure AWS CodeBuild Build and Test the Application

title: Deploy the Application with AWS CodeDeploy
content:
Step 1: Prepare the EC2 Instance Sign in to the AWS Management Console. Open the Amazon EC2 console. Choose Instances and select the instance that will host the Spring Boot application. Verify that the instance is in the Running state. Record the instance ID for later verification. The EC2 instance must have a suitable IAM instance profile, network access to the required AWS services, and the CodeDeploy agent installed and running.
Step 2: Create an IAM Service Role for CodeDeploy Open the IAM console.
Select Roles, then click Create role.
Choose AWS service as the trusted entity type.
Select CodeDeploy as the use case.
Attach the appropriate CodeDeploy service permissions.
Enter the role name:
CodeDeployServiceRole
Choose Create role.
Use the role created for CodeDeploy when configuring the deployment group.
Step 3: Create a CodeDeploy Application Open the AWS CodeDeploy console.
In the navigation pane, choose Applications.
Click Create application.
Enter the application name:
cicd-aws-demo-app
For Compute platform, select EC2/On-premises.
Click Create application.
Step 4: Create a Deployment Group Open cicd-aws-demo-app.
Choose Create deployment group.
Enter the deployment group name:
cicd-aws-demo-deployment-group
Under Service role, select CodeDeployServiceRole.
Under Deployment type, select the deployment option appropriate for the workshop.
Under Environment configuration, select Amazon EC2 instances.
Configure the instance selection criteria using EC2 tags, ensuring the intended application server is selected.
Save the deployment group.
Verify the EC2 tags and deployment group configuration before deploying. Selecting the wrong instances may deploy the application to unintended servers.
Step 5: Prepare the Application Deployment Files Open the local project directory:
cd D:\cicd-aws-demo Check that the project contains the deployment configuration and scripts:
dir dir scripts The project should contain:
appspec.yml — defines the deployment files and lifecycle hooks. scripts/ — contains the scripts used during deployment. pom.xml — defines the Maven build configuration. Check that the script paths and filenames in appspec.yml match the files in the project. The deployment scripts must also have the appropriate permissions and commands for the target EC2 operating system.
Step 6: Deploy the Application Once the application artifact has been generated by AWS CodeBuild and made available to CodeDeploy:
Open the AWS CodeDeploy console. Select the application cicd-aws-demo-app. Open the deployment group cicd-aws-demo-deployment-group. Choose Create deployment. Select the configured revision source and provide the artifact location and revision details required by your deployment configuration. Start the deployment. If the project is orchestrated by AWS CodePipeline, the pipeline can initiate this deployment stage automatically. In that case, use CodePipeline to run the workflow rather than manually creating a separate deployment.
Step 7: Verify the Deployment Status Open the deployment details in the CodeDeploy console. Review the deployment events. Confirm that the deployment status is Succeeded. If the deployment fails, identify the lifecycle event that failed and inspect its logs on the EC2 instance. Common causes include a missing CodeDeploy agent, incorrect IAM permissions, an invalid appspec.yml, missing deployment scripts, or an application startup failure.
Step 8: Test the Web Application After a successful deployment, test the application using the EC2 instance’s public address or the appropriate application endpoint.
For example:
http://<EC2-Public-IP>:8080
Replace <EC2-Public-IP> with the actual public IP address of the instance. This example assumes that the application listens on port 8080 and that the instance is configured to accept the test traffic.
If the page responds as expected, the application is running on the EC2 instance.
Section Summary In this section, you configured AWS CodeDeploy, created a deployment group, and deployed the application artifact to Amazon EC2.
The next step is to integrate the source, build, and deployment stages into AWS CodePipeline so that the application can be deployed automatically when source code changes are detected.

title: Clean Up
content:
Congratulations on completing the Simple Web App CI/CD workshop!
In this workshop, you configured a web application deployment workflow using AWS services. Before finishing, clean up the resources created during the workshop to avoid unnecessary AWS charges.
1. Stop the CI/CD Pipeline Open the AWS CodePipeline console. Select the pipeline created for this workshop. Record the pipeline name for your project report. If the pipeline is no longer needed, delete it from the pipeline details page and confirm the deletion. Deleting a pipeline does not automatically delete all resources associated with it.

title: Sharing and Feedback
content:
During my 10-week internship at First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ), I had the opportunity to explore cloud computing, learn about AWS services, and work toward developing a practical CI/CD project. This experience helped me gain technical knowledge, improve my learning skills, and better understand the working environment in the IT industry.

The internship environment provided opportunities to learn about cloud technologies and develop practical skills. The learning activities and workshop materials helped me become more familiar with AWS services and the CI/CD process. I also had the opportunity to learn independently and explore technical topics at my own pace.
I believe that more group discussions and practical activities would make the learning environment even more engaging and help interns exchange knowledge more effectively.

The guidance and learning resources provided during the program helped me understand unfamiliar technologies and make progress with my internship project. The opportunity to study technical materials and receive feedback was valuable, especially when learning about AWS services and deployment workflows.
I would appreciate having more regular feedback sessions so that interns can identify their weaknesses and improve their work throughout the program.

The internship was relevant to my major in Information Technology, particularly the areas of computer networks, cloud computing, and software deployment.
Through the project “Design and Implementation of an Automated CI/CD Pipeline for Web Application Deployment on AWS,” I had the opportunity to connect my academic knowledge with practical technologies such as Git, GitHub, Spring Boot, Amazon EC2, AWS CodeBuild, AWS CodeDeploy, and AWS CodePipeline.

Besides technical knowledge, I improved my self-learning, research, documentation, and problem-solving skills. These experiences helped me become more confident when approaching unfamiliar technologies.

I believe that more collaborative activities, such as group projects, technical discussions, and knowledge-sharing sessions, would further strengthen connections among interns and program members.

Providing a clearer internship roadmap, regular progress reviews, and more detailed guidance on project requirements would make the experience even more effective for future interns.

The most satisfying part of my internship was having the opportunity to learn about AWS and apply my knowledge to a practical CI/CD project. Understanding how different AWS services work together to automate the deployment of a web application helped me gain a clearer picture of real-world cloud development and operations.
I also appreciated the opportunity to learn independently, explore new technologies, and gradually improve my technical skills.

I think the program could be improved by providing a more detailed learning roadmap, clearer weekly objectives, and more practical exercises for each technical topic.
Regular progress reviews and feedback sessions would also help interns understand whether they are following the right direction and what they need to improve.
3. If recommending to a friend, would you suggest they join this program? Why or why not?
Yes, I would recommend the First Cloud AI Journey program to students who are interested in cloud computing and AWS technologies.
The program offers an opportunity to explore cloud-related knowledge, work on practical learning tasks, and become familiar with technologies that are useful in the IT industry. It is especially suitable for students who are willing to learn independently and actively improve their technical skills.

I would suggest providing more hands-on exercises, practical project examples, and detailed technical documentation. It would also be helpful to organize regular feedback sessions and group discussions so that interns can share their difficulties and learn from one another.
2. Would you like to continue this program in the future?
Yes. I would be interested in continuing to participate in learning activities related to AWS, cloud computing, DevOps, and CI/CD. These areas are valuable for my professional development, and I would like to deepen my knowledge through more advanced projects and practical experience.
3. Any other comments (free sharing):
I would like to express my appreciation to the First Cloud AI Journey program for providing me with the opportunity to learn and develop my technical skills.
The internship helped me understand the importance of continuous learning, practical experience, and self-improvement in the IT industry. Although there are still many areas I need to improve, this experience has given me a clearer direction for my future learning and career development.

title: Clean Up
content:
After completing the CI/CD workshop, remove the AWS resources that are no longer required. This helps prevent unnecessary charges.
Before deleting resources: Save the screenshots and logs needed for the graduation report. Confirm that each resource belongs to this workshop and is not shared with another project.
1. Delete the CodePipeline Pipeline Open the AWS CodePipeline console. Select the pipeline created for cicd-aws-demo. Confirm that you have recorded the pipeline execution results. Delete the pipeline and confirm the action. Deleting the pipeline does not automatically delete its CodeBuild project, CodeDeploy application, S3 artifact bucket, or IAM roles.
2. Delete the CodeDeploy Application Open the AWS CodeDeploy console. Select Applications. Open cicd-aws-demo-app. Delete the deployment group cicd-aws-demo-deployment-group. Delete the application cicd-aws-demo-app. Only delete the application and deployment group created for this workshop.
3. Delete the CodeBuild Project Open the AWS CodeBuild console. Select Build projects. Select cicd-aws-demo-build. Choose Delete build project. Confirm the deletion. The project’s CloudWatch logs and S3 artifacts may remain and must be reviewed separately.
4. Terminate the Workshop EC2 Instance Open the Amazon EC2 console. Select Instances. Identify the instance created for this workshop. Confirm that no other application depends on it. Choose Instance state → Terminate instance and confirm. Termination permanently removes the instance. Review attached EBS volumes, Elastic IP addresses, load balancers, and other related resources separately because some may continue to incur charges.
Do not terminate a shared instance or an instance that hosts other applications.
5. Delete the S3 Artifact Bucket Open the Amazon S3 console. Identify the bucket used for CodePipeline artifacts or deployment packages. Verify that the bucket is dedicated to this workshop. Download any files required for the report. Empty the bucket and delete it if it is no longer needed. If versioning is enabled, remove the necessary object versions and delete markers before deleting the bucket.
Do not delete a bucket shared with other projects.
6. Delete Unneeded CloudWatch Logs Open the Amazon CloudWatch console. Select Logs → Log groups. Identify the log groups created by the workshop. Save any logs needed for documentation. Delete only the log groups that are no longer required. Keep logs from shared applications and services.
7. Review IAM Roles Open the IAM console. Select Roles. Review the roles created for CodeBuild, CodeDeploy, and the EC2 instance. Check whether any remaining resource still uses each role. Delete only unused roles that were created specifically for this workshop. Do not delete shared roles or roles used by other AWS workloads.
8. Verify Cleanup Review the resources created during the workshop.
Resource Expected final state CodePipeline Deleted if no longer needed CodeDeploy application and deployment group Deleted if no longer needed CodeBuild project Deleted if no longer needed EC2 instance Terminated if dedicated to the workshop S3 artifact bucket Deleted if dedicated to the workshop CloudWatch log groups Unneeded logs removed IAM roles Unused workshop-specific roles removed Finally, open AWS Billing and Cost Management and review current charges and remaining billable resources. Billing information may take time to reflect resource deletion.
Result The workshop resources have been reviewed and unnecessary resources have been removed. Evidence of the successful CI/CD workflow has been saved for the graduation report.
